Hi Dora,

This is not a bug. If a a person goes to sleep after midnight and wakes up before noon then the date shown in part 5 is the date on which that sleep window started. If that same person then falls asleep before midnight later that day then also that WW window (next line) is timestamped on the same date. I do this day windows are defined based on waking up times and not based on calendar dates. So, expressing recording days relative to a sequence of calendar dates would not be logical. In the MM analysis where days are defined based on calendar dates the dates should however be a displayed in a logical sequence.

A consequence of this is that days can last much shorter or longer than 24 hours. If you encounter such a day I suggest that you inspect the visualisation of the time series for that person. For individuals with irregular sleep/wake rhythms like shift workers it is not uncommon to see highly irregular day lengths in the WW output. GGIR should have enough measures in place to distinguish true behaviour from measurement artifacts.

If despite this visual check you do not trust the output then you could decide to exclude the specific day(s) for specific recording(s) with argument data_cleaning_file.

Thanks,
Vincent

Hi Dora,

This is not a bug. If a a person goes to sleep after midnight and wakes up before noon then the date shown in part 5 is the date on which that sleep window started. If that same person then falls asleep before midnight later that day then also that WW window (next line) is timestamped on the same date. I do this day windows are defined based on waking up times and not based on calendar dates. So, expressing recording days relative to a sequence of calendar dates would not be logical. In the MM analysis where days are defined based on calendar dates the dates should however be a displayed in a logical sequence.

A consequence of this is that days can last much shorter or longer than 24 hours. If you encounter such a day I suggest that you inspect the visualisation of the time series for that person. For individuals with irregular sleep/wake rhythms like shift workers it is not uncommon to see highly irregular day lengths in the WW output. GGIR should have enough measures in place to distinguish true behaviour from measurement artifacts.

If despite this visual check you do not trust the output then you could decide to exclude the specific day(s) for specific recording(s) with argument data_cleaning_file.

Thanks,
Vincent

Hi Dora,

This is not a bug. If a a person goes to sleep after midnight and wakes up before noon then the date shown in part 5 is the date on which that sleep window started. If that same person then falls asleep before midnight later that day then also that WW window (next line) is timestamped on the same date. I do this day windows are defined based on waking up times and not based on calendar dates. So, expressing recording days relative to a sequence of calendar dates would not be logical. In the MM analysis where days are defined based on calendar dates the dates should however be a displayed in a logical sequence.

A consequence of this is that days can last much shorter or longer than 24 hours. If you encounter such a day I suggest that you inspect the visualisation of the time series for that person. For individuals with irregular sleep/wake rhythms like shift workers it is not uncommon to see highly irregular day lengths in the WW output. GGIR should have enough measures in place to distinguish true behaviour from measurement artifacts.

If despite this visual check you do not trust the output then you could decide to exclude the specific day(s) for specific recording(s) with argument data_cleaning_file.

Thanks,
